On 2026-07-30 I wrote two features and `pi-review` blocked both for the SAME structural error, one I did not recognise the second time even having just been caught on the first.

- **#2340** — read the Behavior identity out of `conversationId` at the MCP gate. That string is assembled from client-supplied request fields, so the "authorization" was a caller-chosen string.
- **#2341** — evaluated a cooldown in `findMatchingBehaviorActivations`, an unlocked SELECT, when the action is actually serialized later by `pg_advisory_xact_lock` inside `createBehaviorEventRun`.

**Why:** In both cases the data I wanted was *conveniently in hand* at the read seam. Convenience of the read site is not evidence it is the decision site.

**How to apply:** Before writing a policy/authorization predicate, answer two questions in this order.
1. **Who authored this value?** Trace it to its construction site, not its type. "It is in a signed token" answers tamper-resistance, not provenance — the gateway may have minted it from a request body. A value the caller supplied cannot authorize the caller.
2. **What already serializes this action?** Find the existing advisory lock / `FOR UPDATE` / queue chokepoint and put the check *there*. If my check runs before the thing that makes the action durable, two replicas race through it.

AGENTS.md already states (2): *"Find the chokepoint that already serializes the action ... and put the check there."* Both blockers were predicted by rules already in the repo — the failure was not reading them as applying to the code I was writing.

Corollary that DID work and is worth keeping: production-faithful test fixtures caught the #2340 id confusion (`tokenData.runId` is the `chat_message` queue row, not the `behavior` run). Manufacture the shape production emits, not the shape the implementation expects.

       if (!match) return false;
       const watcherId = Number(match[1]);
       const behaviorRunId = Number(match[2]);
       if (!Number.isSafeInteger(watcherId) || !Number.isSafeInteger(behaviorRunId)) return false;
       try {
         const sql = db ?? getDb();
         const rows = await sql`
           SELECT w.execution_config->>'permission_mode' AS permission_mode
           FROM watchers w
           JOIN runs behavior_run ON behavior_run.watcher_id = w.id
           WHERE w.id = ${watcherId}
             AND w.organization_id = ${scope.organizationId}
             AND w.agent_id = ${scope.agentId}
             AND behavior_run.id = ${behaviorRunId}
             AND behavior_run.run_type = 'behavior'
             AND behavior_run.organization_id = ${scope.organizationId}
           LIMIT 1
         `;
         const mode = rows[0]?.permission_mode as string | null | undefined;
         return mode != null && UNATTENDED_PERMISSION_MODES.has(mode);
       } catch (error) {
         logger.warn({ error, conversation_id: scope.conversationId },

input.content:
-- migrate:up

-- `min_cooldown_seconds` is the operator's debounce for event-triggered
-- Behaviors. It needs a cursor recording when a Behavior last *activated on an
-- event*, and none of the existing columns mean that:
--
--   * `last_fired_at` is stamped when a run reaches a TERMINAL state
--     (run-lifecycle completion/failure). A burst that starts a run and
--     immediately re-fires would not be debounced by the run it just started,
--     so the cooldown would only take effect after the first run happened to
--     finish.
--   * `runs.created_at` covers background Behaviors but not `reply_to_source`
--     ones — reply targets are routed through the chat transport and never
--     write a `behavior` run row, so the cooldown would be a silent no-op on
--     exactly the Behaviors an operator is most likely to want debounced.
--
-- One cursor, written by both activation paths under the existing
-- per-Behavior advisory lock, keeps a single predicate for a single feature.
-- Deliberately scoped to event activations: a schedule already spaces its own
-- firings (cron IS the operator's cadence control), and suppressing a
-- scheduled firing would strand `next_run_at` in the past and hot-loop.
--
-- Nullable with no backfill: an existing Behavior has no recorded event
-- activation, so its first activation after this deploy is allowed. That is
-- the correct reading of "has not fired within the cooldown window".
ALTER TABLE public.watchers
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS last_event_activation_at timestamp with time zone;

-- migrate:down

ALTER TABLE public.watchers
  DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS last_event_activation_at;

p="packages/server/src/gateway/permissions/unattended-run-policy.ts"
s=open(p).read()
old=''' * WHY conversationId AND NOT `tokenData.runId`: the token's `runId` is the
 * `chat_message` QUEUE row that dispatched the turn, not the parent `behavior`
 * row — `buildRunJobToken` stamps `data.runId` from the queue payload. Joining
 * `runs.watcher_id` on it therefore matches nothing in production. The Behavior
 * identity travels in the signed `conversationId` instead, whose suffix the
 * gateway builds as `_watcher_<watcherId>_run_<behaviorRunId>`. That is the
 * same correlation `listPendingToolsForRun` uses; keep the two in step.
 */'''
new=''' * WHY conversationId AND NOT `tokenData.runId`: the token's `runId` is the
 * `chat_message` QUEUE row that dispatched the turn, not the parent `behavior`
 * row — `buildRunJobToken` stamps `data.runId` from the queue payload. Joining
 * `runs.watcher_id` on it therefore matches nothing in production. The Behavior
 * identity travels in the signed `conversationId` instead, whose suffix the
 * gateway builds as `_watcher_<watcherId>_run_<behaviorRunId>`. That is the
 * same correlation `listPendingToolsForRun` uses; keep the two in step.
 *
 * WHAT MAKES THAT SUFFIX TRUSTWORTHY, and it is not the signature: the token is
 * encrypted, so claims cannot be tampered with AFTER minting, but the gateway
 * mints them from the request body. The suffix is sound because
 * `POST /api/v1/agents` verifies a `behavior_run` intent against server-authored
 * dispatch state and reserves the internal `watcher_<id>` userId prefix — see
 * `./behavior-run-intent.ts`, which owns that invariant and states its residual.
 * If that check is ever weakened, this policy is caller-controlled again.
 */'''
assert old in s
s=s.replace(old,new,1)
open(p,"w").write(s)
print("ok")
PY

## What

`watchers.min_cooldown_seconds` was stored, validated, surfaced in the MCP contract, `defineBehavior`, `lobu apply` and the table schema — and read by **no dispatch predicate**. An operator who set it got no debounce at all.

This wires it at the chokepoint that already serializes a Behavior activation, and makes it work on **both** firing substrates.

## Why the previous revision was drafted

Two blockers, one root cause: the check sat at a read seam instead of the chokepoint.

1. **Lookup/create race.** The cooldown was evaluated in `findMatchingBehaviorActivations`, an unlocked `SELECT`. The actual serializer is `pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('behavior_event_run'), watcherId)` inside `createBehaviorEventRun`, which runs later — so two concurrent deliveries both passed before either run existed.
2. **`reply_to_source` Behaviors accumulated no history.** `planBehaviorActivations` splits reply targets off and the chat bridge routes them through the chat transport, never `createBehaviorEventRun`. No `behavior` run row is written, so a predicate over `runs` was a silent no-op on exactly those Behaviors — a cooldown that works on some Behaviors and silently does nothing on others.

## How

- **New cursor `watchers.last_event_activation_at`** (nullable, no backfill). Neither existing column works: `last_fired_at` is stamped when a run reaches a **terminal** state, so a burst that starts a run and immediately re-fires would not be debounced by the run it just started; `runs.created_at` cannot see reply Behaviors at all.
- **`behaviors/cooldown.ts`** owns the lock and the claim. `createBehaviorEventRun` claims under the lock it already holds; the chat bridge claims through `claimBehaviorCooldownStandalone` for reply targets. One predicate, one cursor, both paths.
- The claim runs **after** dedupe and coalesce: a duplicate delivery and a coalesced signal do not start the Behavior again, so neither consumes the operator's window.
- `MatchingBehaviorActivation.minCooldownSeconds` is carried on the match as a **feature-enabled hint** so a Behavior at the 0 default (the overwhelming majority) costs no extra round-trip and cannot be dropped by a claim that fails closed. The window is still re-read and consumed authoritatively under the lock.
- Event path only, deliberately: cron already spaces scheduled firings, and suppressing one would strand `next_run_at` in the past and hot-loop — exactly what #2326 fixed. Event activations have no cursor to strand.

## What

`execution_config.permission_mode` was validated, role-gated, persisted, shipped to the worker — and read by nobody. A scheduled Behavior has no human to answer the MCP approval card, so the turn burned and failed; the only workaround was a standing `mcp_tool` grant covering every call that agent makes anywhere, far broader than the one Behavior the operator meant to trust.

This makes the field govern the tool-approval gate, and closes the provenance hole that drafted the previous revision.

## Why the previous revision was drafted

The gate read the Behavior's identity out of `tokenData.conversationId`. That string is assembled by the gateway from the **request body**: `CreateAgentRequestSchema` accepts `intent`, `userId` and `thread`, and `POST /api/v1/agents` turns a `behavior_run` intent into `userId = watcher_<behaviorId>` / `thread = run_<runId>`. Signed ≠ trustworthy — the token is encrypted so claims cannot be tampered with *after* minting, but the gateway minted them from caller input, so the signature attests transport integrity, not provenance.

Concretely: a plain member of the org could name any of that agent's Behaviors and inherit its `permission_mode`, even though elevating that field is owner/admin-only at write time.

## How

Verify the intent **once, where it enters the system**, rather than re-deriving provenance at the gate.

`gateway/permissions/behavior-run-intent.ts`:

- **`verifyBehaviorRunIntent`** — the named run must exist, be a `behavior` run of that `behaviorId`, live in the caller's org, and be in the state only the server can write: `claimed_by = 'lobu-dispatcher'` with `status IN ('claimed','running')`. `dispatchWatcherRun` claims the run through `claimPendingWatcherRun` **before** it calls this route and flips it to `running` immediately after, so no API caller can manufacture that state. Fails closed; a rejected intent is a 403, not a downgrade.
- **`isReservedInternalUserId`** — a request body may not supply `watcher_<digits>` as `userId`. Without this the conversation suffix is assemblable with no intent at all, routing around the check entirely.

`unattended-run-policy.ts` keeps its own org + agent + run re-check (defence in depth) and now documents that its soundness rests on the route invariant above.

**Residual, stated plainly:** while a legitimate run of Behavior B is in flight, a member of the same org operating the same agent could name it and inherit B's session shape for that window. Closing that needs a distinguishable service principal at this route — the internal dispatcher token authenticates as an ordinary org owner/admin and the auth middleware surfaces only `userId`/`organizationId`. What *is* closed is the unbounded case: naming any Behavior at any time, including one that has never run. This also hardens the pre-existing forgeable `source: "watcher-run"`, which derives from the same intent.

## Both blockers fixed, both mutation-proven

**#2341 — `min_cooldown_seconds`.** Root cause was one thing, not two: the check sat at a read seam instead of the chokepoint.

The fix moves the claim inside the `pg_advisory_xact_lock` that `createBehaviorEventRun` already holds, and adds a shared cursor `watchers.last_event_activation_at` that *both* firing substrates write. 11	The exact sequence to get a `make task-setup` worktree testable in a browser. Verified 2026-07-29 in `.claude/worktrees/merge-snapshot-evidence` (PORT=9143). Each step below cost a wasted round-trip when skipped.
12	
13	**1. `make build` is a NO-OP — the target you want is `make build-packages`.**
14	`make build` prints "Nothing to be done for `build'" and exits 0, which looks like success. A fresh worktree has no `packages/*/dist`, so until you run `make build-packages` vitest dies at import time with `Failed to resolve entry for package "@lobu/pgvector-embedded"` and then `Failed to load url @lobu/core/contracts/interaction-envelope`. Both are the same missing-dist cause wearing different messages. Related: [[reference_worktree_stale_core_dist]], [[reference_empty_worktree_node_modules_resolves_main]].
15	
16	**2. `make dev` boots ONLY the API.** It runs `packages/server` (`tsx watch src/server.ts`) on the worktree's `.env.local` PORT. It does **not** serve the SPA — `/` and `/index.html` 404 (health reports `"mode":"cloud"`, and in cloud mode the frontend is hosted separately). `packages/owletto/dist/index.html` existing does not change this. Editing server TS is live via tsx watch; no restart needed.
17	
18	**3. The SPA is a second process — vite — and must use `LOBU_API_PROXY`, not `VITE_API_URL`.**
19	```
20	cd packages/owletto && LOBU_API_PROXY=http://127.0.0.1:<API_PORT> \
21	  bun run dev -- --host 127.0.0.1 --port <pick a free one>
22	```
23	`prodApiProxy()` in `vite.config.ts` same-origin-proxies `/api`, `/oauth`, `/connect` and rewrites Set-Cookie (drops Domain, SameSite=None→Lax) so better-auth sessions work. `VITE_API_URL` does NOT work for auth — the config comments say so explicitly.
24	
25	**4. The SPA's backend is the ORIGIN. `/lobu` is the Agent API gateway only.**
26	Setting `VITE_API_URL=.../lobu` yields `GET /lobu/api/auth-config 404` and a "Not signed in" page. Measured on the live server:
27	```
28	/api/auth-config       -> 200
29	/lobu/api/auth-config  -> 404
30	```
31	See [[project_embedded_server_lobu_prefix]] — this is the same split, and it bites the SPA config too.
32	
33	**5. Dev DB is per-branch on 127.0.0.1:5418** (brew postgresql@18), named `lobu_<branch with / and - as _>` — e.g. branch `feat/merge-snapshot-evidence` → `lobu_feat_merge_snapshot_evidence`. Find it with `psql -h 127.0.0.1 -p 5418 -l`. A fresh one has 1 org (`local-install`), 1 user, 0 events — so an empty Activity page is EXPECTED, not a bug. Agents `lobu-builder` + `owletto-default` are seeded, but `inference_providers` is empty, so chat may not resolve a model (see [[reference_org_provider_needs_base_url]]).
34	
35	**6. Integration tests** want `lobu_test`, which is also reachable on 5418:
36	```
37	cd packages/server && DATABASE_URL="postgres://$USER@127.0.0.1:5418/lobu_test" PGSSLMODE=disable \
38	  node ../../node_modules/.bin/vitest run <path> -t "<name>"
39	```
40	
41	**7. To exercise an AGENT-attributed tool call without wiring an LLM** — the useful trick, since the LLM only decides *to call* the tool and everything under test is downstream. Mint a PAT straight into the dev DB (`token = "owl_pat_" + randomBytes(24).toString("base64url")`, `token_hash = sha256(token)` hex, `token_prefix = token.slice(0,12)`, scope `'mcp:read mcp:write mcp:admin'`), then do the MCP streamable-HTTP handshake against `POST /mcp/<orgSlug>`:
42	`initialize` → read the `mcp-session-id` response header → `notifications/initialized` → `tools/call`. Send `x-lobu-agent-id: <agentId>` on every call. `classifyMutationPrincipal` gives `agentId` precedence over `userId`, so the context resolves to kind `"agent"` and takes the approval-gated branch instead of the human fast path. Skipping the handshake returns `Bad Request: Server not initialized`.
43	
44	Do NOT sign in / create the local account yourself — that's the user's step.
45

Then a forged intent over HTTP for the 403.

I'll drive the Behavior creation through MCP with a PAT (the recipe in memory), which exercises the real HTTP surface without needing a model.

Both confirmed — `hashToken` is byte-identical to what `getLobuServiceToken` writes, and `tokenFromHeader` exists. review-fix was right on both counts and I was wrong on both:

1. **There *is* a distinguishable service principal.** I checked `AuthContext.clientId`, found the middleware's narrow context doesn't carry it, and concluded it was unreachable. The raw bearer token was sitting right there — hash it, join `oauth_tokens`, require `client_id = 'lobu-internal'`. That closes the residual I documented as unclosable.
2. **My `userId`-only guard had a real bypass.** `caller_watcher_5` + thread `run_1` assembles the same suffix. Validating the packed `conversationId` is correct; validating one input field was not.

Restoring the load-bearing comments it stripped, then re-verifying:

p="packages/server/src/gateway/permissions/behavior-run-intent.ts"
s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace('''import { hashToken } from "../../auth/oauth/utils.js";''','''/**
 * Server-side verification of a `behavior_run` session intent.
 *
 * `POST /api/v1/agents` accepts `intent: {kind:"behavior_run", runId, behaviorId}`
 * from the request body and turns it into `userId = watcher_<behaviorId>` /
 * `thread = run_<runId>`, hence a conversationId ending
 * `_watcher_<behaviorId>_run_<runId>`. Downstream consumers — the MCP
 * tool-approval gate among them — read a Behavior's identity out of that
 * suffix.
 *
 * Without this check the whole chain is caller-authored. The worker token is
 * encrypted, so its claims cannot be tampered with AFTER minting, but the
 * gateway mints them from the request body: the signature attests transport
 * integrity, not provenance. Verify once, here, where the intent enters the
 * system; never re-derive provenance from the string further down.
 */

import { hashToken } from "../../auth/oauth/utils.js";''',1)
s=s.replace('''const SERVER_DISPATCHER = "lobu-dispatcher";''','''/**
 * `claimPendingWatcherRun`'s `claimedBy` for the server-side Behavior
 * dispatcher. Device-pinned Behaviors are claimed by their worker instead and
 * do not take this route.
 */
const SERVER_DISPATCHER = "lobu-dispatcher";''',1)
open(p,"w").write(s)

Both reviews running. **E2E passed on both — here's where we are.**

## E2E results

Both booted with `make dev` against their own branch Postgres, exercised over real HTTP.

**#2340** — the risk was rejecting the *real* dispatcher, which would stop every Behavior in the product. Created a Behavior over MCP with a PAT, fired it via `manage_behaviors action: trigger` (the actual `dispatchWatcherRun` path):

```
[agent-api] Created API agent: lobu-builder_watcher_1_run_26
[agent-api] Rejected a Behavior-run session: intent does not name a dispatched run
[agent-api] Rejected a session using the reserved Behavior conversation suffix

 id | status  | claimed_by        | error_message
 26 | running | lobu:lobu-builder | (none)
```

The forged request used a **valid PAT for the same org and the same agent**, naming the genuinely in-flight run 26 — refused 403 because it lacks the dispatcher's internal token. That's the residual I'd written off as unclosable, now closed and proven closed.

**#2341** — migration applied cleanly to a fresh branch DB, then two deliveries against two Behaviors sharing one connection and trigger:

```
[cooldown] Suppressing Behavior activation inside its window {"watcherId":1,"cooldownSeconds":1800}
cooldown Behavior fired ONCE across two deliveries — runs=1
cooldown=0 Behavior fired for BOTH deliveries — runs=2
cursor stamped for the cooldown Behavior / untouched at the 0 default
```

The `cooldown=0` line is the one I cared about most — almost every Behavior in production is at that default and must be untouched.

## What I got wrong, and review-fix caught

Worth stating plainly since it changed the design:

- I claimed there was no distinguishable service principal at `/agent`. There is — I checked `AuthContext.clientId`, found the middleware's narrow context lacks it, and stopped instead of noticing the raw bearer token was right there to hash against `oauth_tokens.client_id`.
- My reserved-prefix guard only checked `userId`. `caller_watcher_5` + thread `run_1` assembles the same suffix. Validating the packed `conversationId` is correct.
- On #2341 I had the standalone claim swallow DB errors and return "suppressed" — silently dropping a user's message. Propagating is both the AGENTS rule and consistent with the background half of the same handler, which already throws.

I also rewrote three tests review-fix added: they asserted a 400 for inputs that can't actually form the suffix (the org id gets interleaved), so they were testing the mechanism rather than the property. They now assert the invariant — no unverified session ever carries the correlation — which holds regardless of which mechanism fires.

One process slip: I fired `make review` twice from the same directory. The duplicate-run guard refused the second (`already running (pid 91180); duplicate refused`), so no review cycle was burned.

## Remaining

`make review` on both, then merge on green. I won't `--admin` past a check that hasn't reported.

**Confidence: 93 / 90** (#2341 / #2340) — up from 88/80, because the normal path is now verified on a booted server rather than assumed. The gap on both: #2341's `reply_to_source` half is covered by a stubbed bridge test plus a DB-level claim test, not a live Slack workspace, and #2340's MCP gate allowing an unattended call was tested at the integration layer, not end-to-end with a real worker turn.

**#2341 merged. #2340 had a real blocker — fixed, not merged yet.**

## The blocker was legitimate and it's my mistake a third time

Codex: *"authorizes unattended tools from the conversation-id suffix alone; a same-agent direct/API turn or reused Behavior session can inherit `bypassPermissions`."* Its probe confirmed `runAllowsUnattendedToolUse` returned true for `source=direct-api` with a matching suffix.

I guarded session **creation** and assumed that covered it. It doesn't — a Behavior conversation outlives the dispatch that created it. An ordinary org member posting a second message into the dispatcher's live session, or opening a direct-API turn on the same conversation, inherits the elevated mode. **The escalation is per-turn; I put the check per-session.**

Same root cause as the first two blockers, third variation: I keep placing the check one level away from the thing being authorized.

**The fix** binds to `runs.dispatched_message_id` — written by `dispatchWatcherRun` in the same statement that marks the run `running`, before it posts the message the worker token is minted from. The gate now requires `dispatched_message_id = tokenData.messageId` and `status = 'running'`. That's the server-authored fact identifying the one turn the dispatcher started.

It also makes the reviewer's second suggested fix (guard the message-post route) unnecessary — an extra message gets its own `messageId`, so it simply doesn't match.

```
MUTATION: dropped dispatched_message_id →  2 failed | 14 passed
MUTATION: dropped status = 'running'   →  1 failed | 15 passed
reverted                               → 16 passed
```

Full MCP suite: **121 passed, 2 skipped**.

## Second process slip

I mutated an **uncommitted** fix, then `git checkout --` to revert the mutation — which deleted the fix. My own memory note says *commit BEFORE mutating*. Caught it immediately (4 tests went red), re-applied, committed, then re-ran the mutations properly against the committed version.

## Where we are

| | #2341 | #2340 |
|---|---|---|
| **Merged** | ✅ `b348aa89` | ⛔ |
| pi-review | ✅ 0 blockers, 87 | ⚠️ 1 blocker → fixed, needs re-review |
| e2e | ✅ | ✅ (predates this fix) |

Honest note on the e2e: it passed *before* this blocker was found, and it didn't catch it, because I only tested the dispatcher's own turn — not a second turn on the same conversation. The new integration cases cover that; I have not re-run the booted-server e2e against the new binding.

`make pre-pr` is running. Then push and one more `make review`. Given three design errors of the same shape on this PR, I'd rather it get a clean verdict than push it through — I won't merge #2340 on a low score or an unresolved finding.

cat >> packages/server/src/gateway/permissions/unattended-run-policy.ts <<'EOF'

/**
 * A Behavior turn asked for unattended tool use and did not get it. Say so.
 *
 * The gate is deliberately narrow, so there are legitimate misses (an
 * interactive turn on a Behavior conversation). But one miss is a FALSE
 * AFFORDANCE and must not be silent: a device-pinned Behavior is claimed by
 * `worker-api/poll.ts`, which never writes `dispatched_message_id` — only the
 * server dispatcher in `watchers/automation.ts` does. So an operator can set
 * `permission_mode` on a device Behavior, have it accepted and persisted, and
 * get no effect at all. That is the exact class of dead config this policy
 * exists to remove, so it is logged rather than swallowed until the device
 * poll records a per-turn correlation of its own.
 *
 * Costs a query only when the conversation really is a Behavior turn AND the
 * bind already failed — never on an ordinary chat turn.
 */
async function logUnattendedBindMiss(
	sql: DbClient,
	watcherId: number,
	behaviorRunId: number,
	scope: UnattendedRunScope,
): Promise<void> {
	const diagnostic = await sql`
    SELECT w.execution_config->>'permission_mode' AS permission_mode,
           w.device_worker_id IS NOT NULL AS device_pinned,
           behavior_run.status AS run_status,
           behavior_run.dispatched_message_id IS NULL AS never_dispatched
    FROM watchers w
    LEFT JOIN runs behavior_run
      ON behavior_run.id = ${behaviorRunId}
     AND behavior_run.watcher_id = w.id
    WHERE w.id = ${watcherId}
      AND w.organization_id = ${scope.organizationId}
    LIMIT 1
  `;
	const row = diagnostic[0];
	const mode = row?.permission_mode as string | null | undefined;
	if (mode == null || !UNATTENDED_PERMISSION_MODES.has(mode)) return;
	logger.warn(
		{
			behavior_id: watcherId,
			behavior_run_id: behaviorRunId,
			permission_mode: mode,
			device_pinned: row?.device_pinned === true,
			run_status: row?.run_status ?? null,
			never_dispatched_by_server: row?.never_dispatched !== false,
		},
		"[mcp] Behavior declares unattended execution but this turn is not its recorded server dispatch — requiring approval",
	);
}
EOF

content.text:
**#2341 merged. #2340 in review round 3.**

## The blocker was real and it was my mistake a third time

Codex found that the gate still authorized from the conversation-id suffix alone — its own probe confirmed `direct-api` turns got through. I had guarded session *creation* and assumed that settled it. It doesn't: **a Behavior conversation outlives the dispatch that created it**. Any later turn on it — an org member's second message, a direct-API call — inherited `bypassPermissions`.

Three variations of one error now: check at a read seam (#2340 v1), check before the serializer (#2341), check at the wrong granularity (#2340 v2). Each time I keyed on something adjacent to the thing being authorized rather than the thing itself.

**The fix** binds to `runs.dispatched_message_id` — written by `dispatchWatcherRun` in the same statement that marks the run `running`, before the message the token is minted from. Plus `status = 'running'`. That's the narrowest server-authored artifact for exactly this turn, and it existed already; I'd been inventing weaker proxies instead of looking for it. It also removes the need for the reviewer's second suggested fix, since an extra turn carries its own `messageId`.

```
dropped dispatched_message_id →  2 failed | 14 passed
dropped status = 'running'    →  1 failed | 15 passed
reverted                      → 16 passed
full MCP suite                → 121 passed | 2 skipped
```

Verified on the booted gateway's DB that a real dispatch populates the column (`789f88b1-964b…`).

## One thing I found that the reviewer didn't

Only `automation.ts` writes `dispatched_message_id`. Device-pinned Behaviors are claimed by `worker-api/poll.ts`, which doesn't — so `permission_mode` is inert for them. Not a regression (the field did nothing anywhere before), but a silently-dead config is precisely what this PR exists to eliminate, so a miss now logs with `device_pinned` and `never_dispatched_by_server`. The diagnostic query only runs when it's genuinely a Behavior turn *and* the bind already failed.

## Second process slip

I mutation-tested an **uncommitted** fix, then reverted the mutation with `git checkout --` — which deleted the fix. My own memory rule says commit first. Caught it when 4 tests went red, re-applied, committed, re-ran the mutations properly.

## Status

| | #2341 | #2340 |
|---|---|---|
| **Merged** | ✅ `b348aa89` | ⛔ in review |
| pi-review | ✅ 87, 0 blockers | round 3 running |

Memory updated with the three-strikes pattern and a third diagnostic question — *what is the granularity of the thing being authorized?* — plus the commit-before-mutating note.

**Owed:** prod-verify for #2341 against squash `b348aa89`. I'll set the rollout gate once #2340 resolves so both go in one pass. I won't merge #2340 on an unresolved finding.

## What

`POST /api/v1/agents` accepts `intent: {kind:"behavior_run", runId, behaviorId}` from the request body and turns it into `userId = watcher_<behaviorId>` / `thread = run_<runId>`, producing a `conversationId` ending `_watcher_<id>_run_<id>`. Nothing verified that intent, and nothing stopped an ordinary caller assembling the same suffix out of `userId`/`thread` directly.

That suffix is a correlation downstream code reads a Behavior's identity out of, and `source: "watcher-run"` is derived from the same unverified intent. **Signed ≠ trustworthy**: the worker token is encrypted, so its claims cannot be tampered with *after* minting, but the gateway mints them from the request body — the signature attests transport integrity, not provenance.

## How

`gateway/permissions/behavior-run-intent.ts`:

- **`verifyBehaviorRunIntent`** — the named run must exist, be a `behavior` run of that `behaviorId`, live in the caller's org, and be `claimed_by = 'lobu-dispatcher'` with `status = 'claimed'` — state only `claimPendingWatcherRun` writes, before this route is called. **And** the request must carry the dispatcher's short-lived internal OAuth token (`oauth_tokens.client_id = 'lobu-internal'`), because run state alone is not a capability: a same-org member can observe or guess an in-flight run id. Fails closed; a rejected intent is a 403.
- **`parseBehaviorRunConversationId`** — the reserved-suffix guard runs on the **assembled `conversationId`**, not on individual request fields. Guarding `userId` alone is bypassable: `caller_watcher_5` + thread `run_1` reassembles the suffix, as does packing it entirely into either field.

This branch previously also made `execution_config.permission_mode` govern the MCP tool-approval gate. **That has been removed and deferred to its own PR.** Four review rounds each found a genuine bypass in it, and the last one is not patchable at this layer: there is no unforgeable per-turn provenance today. `messageId` looked like one but is caller-supplied (`const messageId = body.messageId || randomUUID()`), and turns reach a conversation through seven distinct `enqueueMessage` call sites, so no single entry-point guard is a chokepoint either. That's a design problem, and the design answer was in my own first analysis this session — *carry an unforgeable minted claim* — which I talked myself out of as too big. It was the right call.

That pre-pr failure was a false alarm worth naming: the owletto submodule in this worktree had drifted to a per-task branch, and `make task-setup` had left the pinned SHA unfetched. My HEAD and `origin/main` pin the identical commit, so CI would never have seen it. Synced to the pin; rerunning.

Recording it, since it'll recur in any long-lived worktree:

input.content:
---
name: reference_worktree_submodule_drift_fails_pre_pr
description: "A stale packages/owletto checkout in a task worktree fails make pre-pr with a frontend tsc error that CI will never see"
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`make pre-pr` builds the **checked-out** `packages/owletto`, not the SHA the branch pins. In a worktree that has been alive a while, `make task-setup` leaves the submodule on a per-task branch that drifts, so pre-pr fails with a frontend error in a file the PR never touched.

Seen 2026-07-30 on PR #2340 (3 server files, zero frontend):

```
src/components/agents/skill-editor.tsx(35,26): error TS2339:
  Property 'nixPackages' does not exist on type ...
make: *** [pre-pr] Error 2
```

**Diagnose before fixing anything** — the failure is real output, but it may be local-only:

```
git submodule status packages/owletto     # leading '+' = working tree != pinned SHA
git ls-tree HEAD packages/owletto         # what my branch pins
git ls-tree origin/main packages/owletto  # what main pins
```

If HEAD and `origin/main` pin the **same** SHA and the PR touches no frontend, the error cannot reach CI — CI checks out the pin. Fix locally:

```
cd packages/owletto && git fetch -q origin && git checkout <pinned-sha>
```

The pinned commit is often **not even present locally** (`fatal: Not a valid commit name`), so the `git fetch` is load-bearing — same reason [[feedback_absence_needs_origin_main_grep]] insists on it.

**Do NOT reset the submodule blindly.** `AGENTS.md`'s `ensure-submodule` warns on drift instead of auto-fixing because the drift may be another task's active feature work. Check `git status --porcelain` inside the submodule first; only reset when it is clean and the PR genuinely owns no frontend change.

If HEAD and `origin/main` pin *different* SHAs, this is a real cross-repo ordering problem instead — see [[reference_submodule_merge_order]] (owletto PR merges FIRST) and [[feedback_owletto_web_submodule]].

**#2341 is live in prod** — deployed revision `db32432a` contains `b348aa89`. But the verification turned up something you should see.

## Prod verification: partial, and one finding

What I can confirm:
- **Deployed** — merge-base gate passed against the squash commit.
- **Migration applied** — `min_cooldown_seconds` reads cleanly; the schema is intact.
- **Scheduler alive after the deploy** — Behavior 5 shows `updated_at 02:00:47Z` and `next_run_at` advancing to `03:00Z`, roughly an hour post-rollout. #2341 didn't break scheduling.

What I can't confirm, and won't claim: **the event-path cooldown is not exercised in prod.** There's no event-triggered Behavior with a cooldown set, and completions stopped at `23:00:47Z` on 07-29 — about two hours *before* the merge, so that silence is pre-existing (the tracked z.ai quota issue), not something I caused. I checked the timing specifically because "no completions since deploy" would otherwise have looked like my regression.

**The finding worth your attention:** the only Behavior in prod with `min_cooldown_seconds` set is `hourly-task-collaborator` (id 5), at **300 seconds** — and it's **schedule**-triggered. #2341 deliberately wires the cooldown to the event path only, because suppressing a scheduled firing strands `next_run_at` and hot-loops. So the single real user of this field gets nothing from the fix I just shipped.

That's the same false-affordance pattern, now visible in production data. Whoever set 300 there expected throttling. Options: surface it in the UI/contract as event-only, reject the field at write time for schedule-only Behaviors, or solve the scheduled case properly with cursor-advance-on-suppression. That's a product call, not mine.

Making `execution_config.permission_mode` govern the MCP tool-approval gate was **deferred out of PR #2340** on 2026-07-30 after four consecutive `pi-review` rounds, each finding a real bypass. #2340 shipped only the `/agent` hardening. `permission_mode` stays inert, as on main — no regression, workaround is still a broad standing `mcp_tool` grant.

**Every attempt keyed on something a caller can influence:**

| round | keyed on | why it failed |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `tokenData.runId` | that is the `chat_message` QUEUE row, not the `behavior` run — matches nothing in prod |
| 2 | `conversationId` suffix | assembled by the gateway from request-body `intent`/`userId`/`thread` |
| 3 | suffix + verified intent at `/agent` | verifies the SESSION; the escalation is per-TURN, and a session outlives its dispatch |
| 4 | `runs.dispatched_message_id` = `tokenData.messageId` | `const messageId = body.messageId \|\| randomUUID()` — caller-supplied and exposed in SSE, so replayable while the run is live |

**Why there is no fifth attribute.** A turn reaches a conversation through **seven** `enqueueMessage` call sites (`manage_conversations`, `scheduled/jobs`, `chat-instance-manager`, `message-handler-bridge`, `gateway/api/platform`, `routes/public/agent`, `services/agent-threads`). No single entry-point guard is a chokepoint, so "restrict who may post to a Behavior session" does not close it either.

**The design that does work** (unbuilt): stamp dispatch provenance at ENQUEUE time, derived from the authenticated principal, never read from a request body — `enqueueMessage({..., dispatchProvenance})` set only when the caller IS the internal dispatcher (`oauth_tokens.client_id = 'lobu-internal'`). Carry it on `WorkerTokenData`, minted by `buildRunJobToken` from the queue row. The gate then reads a claim no caller ever authored. Do a design review BEFORE implementing — see [[feedback_design_review_before_implementing]].

**Also unresolved, found during prod verification:** the only prod Behavior with `min_cooldown_seconds` set is `hourly-task-collaborator` (id 5, 300s) and it is SCHEDULE-triggered, so the merged #2341 cooldown does nothing for it (event-path only, deliberately — see [[project_min_cooldown_seconds_event_only]]). Same false-affordance shape, visible in production. Needs a product call: surface it as event-only, reject the field for schedule-only Behaviors, or build cursor-advance-on-suppression.

Device-pinned Behaviors have the same gap for `permission_mode`: only `watchers/automation.ts` writes `dispatched_message_id`; `worker-api/poll.ts` claims device Behavior runs and does not.

See [[feedback_put_the_check_at_the_chokepoint]], [[reference_behavior_conversation_id_is_client_forgeable]], [[project_behavior_run_sdk_approval_gate]].

**Both PRs are merged.**

| PR | Squash | Review | Prod |
|---|---|---|---|
| #2341 `min_cooldown_seconds` | `b348aa89` | 87, 0 blockers | ✅ live |
| #2340 `/agent` intent hardening | `10160927` | 86, 0 blockers, `tests_adequate` | rollout gate polling |

Both merged only after all 9 required checks reported — no `--admin` past a pending check. The rollout poller will tell me when #2340 lands.

## What actually shipped

**#2341** wires `min_cooldown_seconds` at the advisory-lock chokepoint with a shared `last_event_activation_at` cursor that both firing substrates write, so it isn't a debounce on background Behaviors and a silent no-op on reply ones.

**#2340** verifies `behavior_run` intent against dispatcher-authored state *plus* the internal OAuth client, and reserves the Behavior conversation suffix on the assembled id. That closes the pre-existing forgeable `source: "watcher-run"`.

## What I cut, and why that's the important part

`permission_mode` governing the tool-approval gate is **not shipped**. Four review rounds, four genuine bypasses, each because I keyed the gate on something a caller can influence — `runId`, then the conversation suffix, then session-level intent, then `messageId` (which is literally `body.messageId || randomUUID()`).

I stopped at four rather than reaching for a fifth, because the audit showed there's nothing left to reach for: seven `enqueueMessage` sites mean no entry-point guard is a chokepoint either. The fix is enqueue-time provenance derived from the authenticated principal and carried as a token claim — which was in my first analysis this session, and I wrongly judged too big. Written up with the full failure table so the next attempt starts from the design, not another attribute.

I also dropped the contract-description change with it. Describing a bypass that doesn't exist would have recreated the exact false affordance this work set out to remove.

## Two things from prod verification you should see

**Behavior 5 (`hourly-task-collaborator`) has `min_cooldown_seconds = 300` on a *schedule* trigger** — so the feature I just shipped does nothing for the only prod Behavior that uses the field. That's event-path-only by design (suppressing a scheduled firing strands `next_run_at`), but it's the false-affordance pattern showing up in live data. Needs a product call.

**Prod Behaviors haven't completed since 23:00Z on 07-29** — about two hours *before* #2341 merged, so not caused by it. I checked the timing specifically because it would otherwise have read as my regression. Second occurrence of the tracked quota issue; worth its own look.

## Honest confidence

**#2341: 90.** e2e-verified on a booted gateway, mutation-proven, live in prod — but the `reply_to_source` half has never run against a real chat workspace, and prod currently has no event Behavior with a cooldown, so that path is untested in production.

**#2340: 88.** e2e-verified, every predicate mutation-killed, clean review at reduced scope. Lower than the test evidence alone suggests, because this PR's earlier scope failed review four times and I'd rather be under-confident here.

Memory updated: the merges, the deferred-gate design with its failure table, the three-strikes chokepoint lesson (plus a new question — *what granularity is being authorized?*), commit-before-mutating, and the worktree submodule-drift trap that made pre-pr fail on a file I never touched.
